list.listitem: The complete blood count and leukocyte differential count have no value in screening asymptomatic members of the general population. C
If infection is clinically evident, a leukocyte differential count is unnecessary to confirm the diagnosis in most cases. C

Peripheral blood smear is helpful to determine etiology of leukocytosis in cases where cancer or myeloproliferative disorders may be suspected. Bone marrow biopsy should be done to confirm a diagnosis of cancer or myeloproliferative disorders if indicated by peripheral blood smear results. C

background.definition: The normal white blood cell (WBC) count in adults varies from 4,400 to 11,000 cells per microliter. Leukocytosis is defined as a white blood cell count greater than 11,000 per mm3. Leokocytosis is most commonly due to an increase in the absolute number of mature neutrophils.

list.listitem: See Differential Diagnosis table and .
Leukocytosis may occur as a result of one of two mechanisms: (1) normal bone marrow reacting to an external stimulus such as inflammation or infection or (2) abnormal bone marrow (i.e., malignancy).

The most common causes of leukocytosis are secondary to inflammation or infection. In both of these situations, circulating polymorphonuclear leukocytes, band cells, and metamyelocytes move to the site of injury or infection.
Other causes of leukocytosis include physical and or emotional stress.
Certain medications such as lithium, corticosteroids and beta agonists can also lead to leukocytosis.
Splenectomy, hemolytic anemia, and malignancy can all present with leukocytosis. The mechanism of increased white blood cell count is due to non-specific bone marrow stimulation.

Differential.Differential_Features: History and physical exam findings consistent with infection (fever, chills, abdominal pain, abscess, etc.)
History and physical exam findings consistent with inflammatory disease (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, vasculitis, Kawasaki syndrome)
Recent, significant emotional or physical stress
Use of lithium, corticosteroids, heparin, or beta-blockers
Jaundice or splenomegaly may be present
Myeloblasts or lymphoblasts seen on peripheral smear
Auer Rods on peripheral blood smear
Hyperlobulated nuclei on peripheral blood smear
Smudge cells on peripheral blood smear

Differential.Differential_Name: Familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome (familial cold urticaria)
Differential.Differential_Features: Purpuric lesions a few hours following cold exposure; fever, chills, joint pains, and neutrophilia follow
Ragged cytoplasm on peripheral blood smear

list.listitem: Ask the patient about any signs of active infection, such as respiratory symptoms, urinary symptoms, abdominal pain, vomiting, or diarrhea. Also any history of fever, chills, or night sweats.
Note any history or presence of anxiety, depression, or emotional stress.
Ask about cigarette smoking, recent trauma, injury, or burn. Also ask about a history of hematologic diseases, splenectomy or asplenia.
Ask about recent medication use, especially recent antibiotics (post-antibiotic diarrhea), corticosteroids, beta-blockers, or lithium.
Vital signs to assess for fever, hypotension, shock, tachycardia.
General examination for rash, adenopathy, abscess or evidence of infection at any site.
Abdominal exam: pain, mass, localized tenderness, hepatosplenomegaly, absent bowel sounds or other peritoneal signs.
Lung exam: any evidence of pulmonary consolidation or pleural effusion.
Musculoskeletal: joint swelling, erythema, tenderness.

In patients with unexplained leukocytosis, obtain an automated differential. If abnormal, obtain a manual differential count. Most leukocytosis is secondary to neutrophilia (i.e., a 'left shift'). However, leukocytosis could also be due to lymphocytosis, eosinophilia, monocytosis, and very rarely basophilia. See for differential diagnosis based on the manual differential count.
Peripheral blood smear should be obtained when a patient has persistent elevation in WBC and no clear signs of infection. See for interpretation of cell types in the peripheral smear.

C-reactive protein (CRP) is a marker of inflammation and may elevated in patients with inflammatory causes of leukocytosis such as rheumatoid arthritis and vasculitis, acute pancreatitis, and cardiovascular disease. CRP is moderately accurate as a test for serious bacterial infection in febrile patients under age 18.

A systematic review found 8 studies with 1883 in young children age 7 days to 36 months presenting with fever and no clear source, comparing procalcitonin, CRP and leukocytosis. The strongest association with serious bacterial infection was for procalcitonin (OR 10.6), followed by CRP (OR 9.8), followed by leukocytosis (OR 4.3).

Bone marrow testing along with specific histochemical staining should be done to confirm the diagnosis when malignancy or myeloproliferative disorders are suspected based on the WBC count, manual differential, and peripheral blood smear.
Leukocytosis is only moderately helpful in diagnosing appendicitis, meningitis, and cholecystitis.
A retrospective review of 847 appendectomies in children found that 22 were negative, and of those, 89% had a normal white blood count.
Leukocytosis is an independent predictor of MRSA bacteremia and was incorporated in a clinical decision rule.

In patients with acute non-traumatic abdominal pain not suspected of having either appendicitis or renal colic, leukocytosis (OR 3.3) and relative lymphopenia (OR 3.8) were the best independent predictors of significant pathology on CT.
Please refer to algorithm in for a suggested approach to evaluation of the patient with unexplained leukocytosis.
